title: Photograph - Hermann Zentner picking pears, Shepparton, Victoria, 1941-1942
CreCreationNotes:
Black and white photograph depicting Dunera internee Hermann Zentner picking pears in the JGB & R McDonald orchard, located in Central Avenue, Shepparton East. Hermann Zentner later remained in Australia and received his naturalisation on 7 August 1946.
The orchard belonged to Sir John Gladstone Black McDonald (6 December 1898 – 23 April 1977) who was Deputy Premier of Victoria from November 1947 to December 1948 and later served as the 37th Premier of Victoria (leading the Country Party) from 27 June 1950 to 17 December 1952.
McDonald was born in Scotland and emigrated to Australia with his family in 1912, settling in Shepparton and establishing a dairy farm with orchards. During World War II, farmers were short of fruit pickers, so some Tatura internees were sent to help. 
According to Mary Allison’s (McDonald’s daughter), recollections: “The Dunera internees must have been on the orchard in late November 1941 and into the New Year of 1942. Whilst on the orchard, these men lived in the loft of the large corrugated ‘shed’ – as it was called by everyone. The Dunera men were not permitted to leave the property. When they were staying at the shed, they compiled food lists and the women bought food for them in the town. As there were Jewish families on orchards in the district, there was a small synagogue and a place for the correct preparation of Kosher meat, so it was possible for the men to have meat. […] My most wonderful memory of the Dunera Boys was their Sunday nights in our home. We were fortunate enough to have a piano in Dad’s office. When the Dunera Boys were with us, they were invited to the house for musical evenings. Unfortunately I do not know which ones treated us to such marvellous concerts, however there were times when they sang as they picked fruit”.

CreCreationNotes: This programme was handmade by Fritz Schönbach c. 1941, for a production staged by the Dunera Boys at the Tatura internment camp. The Story of the Good Soldier Schwejk was part of a wide cultural movement that flourished in the camp, in spite of its appalling conditions. Younger internees managed to continue their studies via correspondence, sporting teams were formed, and adult education and entertainment prospered. Men with special skills were also given restricted release into organizations and industry.

CreCreationNotes: This program was made on board of the Dunera ship in its way from Australia back to Liverpool. The programme is printed, black text on a white card ground, with a coloured image printed on the front cover. Handwritten notes outlining the voyage and it's stops, are on the back cover, in blue ink. This is a program for a variety of shows and musicals titled "We're in love!!!" produced by Capt. O'Gorman, Peter Land and Ray Martin. On the voyage from Australia to Liverpool the entertainment committee presented a variety ship's concert in the first class lounge. The ship went from Australia, through Auckland, then through Panama Canal where some internees were released early, and then to Liverpool. This specific concert was held on November 11th 1941, at 2:30 and 8:15 p.m. The dance in the show was devised by Max Lewinsky, and the music written and arranged by Ray Martin. The stage manager for this show was Bernard Bell.

CreCreationNotes:
This item is a programme for the "Sergeant Snow White" musical revue held at the Union Theatre in Melbourne on April 15, 17 and 19 in 1943. The musical was staged to celebrate the first anniversary of the 8th Employment Company and members of the Company appeared in the play. The play featured a portrayal of "Hitler as the Big Bad Wolf and with other contemporary references". It was written and directed by Sergeant Doc. K. Sternberg who was an internationally renowned film producer. Following the war, he worked in film production in Australia, including the story of the Borovansky Ballet. The programme's cover image was drawn by Erwin Fabian who was a graphic design artist during and after the war. He returned to England where he continued to work as a graphic and industrial artist but came back to Melbourne in 1960. He has since become a successful and respect sculptor whose work is represented in the National Gallery of Victoria, the High Court and Parliament House.

Klaus Loewald, a performer in the play, recalled that "members of the cast were continually recognised in the streets when on leave".

narratives_resolved.description:
Since the First Fleet arrived in Botany Bay in 1788, Jewish people have made important contributions within Australian public life as leaders, politicians, soldiers, activists, philanthropists, in business and in the arts.

This area of the collection provides an insight into what makes Australia’s community distinct from other Jewish communities around the world and how being Australian has influenced the lives of Jewish people since colonisation.

The objects, artworks and documents included explore the following questions; What is uniquely Australian about our Jewish way of life and our community? How do Jews feel about being Australian? How does being an Australian Jew manifest itself in our lives, our work, our art or writings?

This collection theme also covers the historical background of the Australian Jewish community, with a particular focus on Melbourne. Migration stories are encapsulated by letters, documents and objects. The continuation of Jewish traditions in Australia is also exemplified through documents and objects, which reveal profound connections to religious and cultural practices as well as the Australian way of life.

SummaryData: "Booklet - Booklet of songs for Oneg Shabbat, Tatura, Victoria, 1941" [4057]
CreCreationNotes:
This 8-page typed booklet contains songs traditionally sung during Oneg Shabbat, the joyous and entertaining celebration held on Friday evenings to express happiness for Shabbat. Groups and families gather in houses or synagogues to enjoy music, drama, community discussions, lectures, or the singing of religious melodies. The songs typed in black ink in this booklet are in Hebrew and translated in German. The front cover reveals the date (1941) and the content of the booklet: Hebrew songs to be sung during Shabbat in Tatura. The front cover is also decorated with a Star of David and an altar with two candlesticks and a Kiddush cup. 
It is likely that this booklet was created at Tatura Internment Camp by Jewish internees in order to be able to sing jointly during the Shabbat celebration.

Life at Hay was made as bearable as conditions allowed. Boredom was overcome by paid work, hobbies, sport and camp entertainment. This is a programme for a concert held at the Hay Camp, directed and arranged by M. Pietruschka. The concert featured the works of Delibres, Czibulka, Rimsky-Korsakov, Brahms, Dvorak, Boccherin, Gounod, Paganini and Strauss. Performers included M. Pietruschka (violin), Mr. Chlumecky (violin), Mr Silberstein (violin), Mr Goldmann-Petersen (violin), Mr Landauer (guitar), Mr Gurland (flute) and Mr Ehrenzweig (bass). Mr. S Cohn was the manager of the concert, while Mr E. Wittenberg was the stage manager. Mr Ehrenzweig also sang two ballads, "Prince Eugen" and "The Campbells are Commin'".

Russian-born Ivan Pietruschka was a talented violinist and conductor in Eastern Europe. In 1939 he sought refuge in England, but was soon declared an “enemy alien” by the British and sent to Australia on the H.M.T Dunera with approximately 2000 other Jewish refugees of German and Austrian descent. Interned with other refugees at Hay Camp, Ivan performed regular concerts alongside other interned musicians, Peter Stadlen and Hans Werner Katz. Ivan joined the 8th Employment Company in 1942, created so internees could help with the war effort, before being discharged in 1943. In 1952, Ivan joined the Victorian Symphony Orchestra, now a naturalised Australian.

CreCreationNotes: Russian-born Ivan Pietruschka was a talented violinist and conductor in Eastern Europe. In 1939 he sought refuge in England, but was soon declared an “enemy alien” by the British and sent to Australia on the H.M.T Dunera with approximately 2000 other Jewish refugees of German and Austrian descent. Interned with other refugees at Hay Camp, Ivan performed regular concerts alongside other interned musicians, Peter Stadlen and Hans Werner Katz. Ivan joined the 8th Employment Company in 1942, created so internees could help with the war effort, before being discharged in 1943. In 1952, Ivan joined the Victorian Symphony Orchestra, now a naturalised Australian.
